sections.title: The study of politics
sections.html:
The word politics comes from the Greek polis, the city-state. Ancient Greece was made up of several city-states, Athens the biggest, so the study of politics is traced back to Ancient Greece.

Definitions of politics

DefinitionWhat it meansWeakness or note
The art of the possibleYou cannot achieve all your aims, so you scale them down. Politics is compromise and consensus: resolving conflict by negotiation and conciliation rather than force.—
Governing of menPolitics revolves around the governed and those who govern.In the past only chiefs took part in government
Struggle for powerThe ordinary person's view: the struggle for, and exercise of, power and influence.—
Who gets what, when, how and whyPolitics decides who benefits.Especially real in Africa, where office is used to acquire wealth
Authoritative allocation of valuesThe distribution of resources (David Easton's definition).Ignores production: what do you distribute that you do not produce?
State powerA president commands with the police, army and bureaucracy behind him; an archbishop can only pray.Separates political from other kinds of power
Public affairsDistinguishes the public from the private sphere; politics as an ethical activity creating a just society.—

Working definition: politics is all activities directly or indirectly associated with the seizure of state power, its consolidation (obedience without coercion) and its use.

Aristotle, founder of the discipline, called politics the "master science", because it is the activity through which people try to improve their lives and create a just society. He said "man is by nature a political animal". Everything happens in a political context: a hurricane is natural, but deciding where to build dikes and which victims to help is political.

Political science as a social science

Political science sits beside economics, sociology and social psychology. It studies political behaviour, institutions and processes in the public realm. Its sub-disciplines:

  • Comparative politics: comparing political systems of similar or different countries (e.g. Botswana and South Africa).
  • International relations: international politics (relations between countries) and international law and organisations. It grew after World War II from the wish to build a better world and prevent another major war.
  • Political theory: the basis of the discipline. It deals with concepts, ideas and values, asking what ought to be rather than what is: what is good government?
  • Public administration: administering policies set by the legislature, executive and judiciary, carried out by the bureaucracy.
  • Public law: the judicial process, the making and enforcing of laws.
  • Public policy: all the laws, rules and regulations a political system produces, from formulation to implementation.

Can the study of politics be objective?

Behaviouralists argue science provides (1) reliable, objective facts and (2) general laws that explain them. Facts must be verifiable by any impartial observer, so the researcher must stay value-free. This is hard because politics is about power and values, and we are all personally involved.

Good political analysis is reasoned (states its assumptions), balanced (acknowledges other approaches and the literature), supported by evidence (quantitative and qualitative, even secondary) and theoretical (confirms or refutes theory). Political science can "speak truth to power".

Politicians…Political scientists…
love powerare sceptical about power
seek popularityseek accuracy
think practicallythink abstractly
seek short-term payoffseek long-term consequences
seek recognitionseek professional growth
plan for the next electionplan for the next publication

Uses of political science: teaching, a political career, the bureaucracy, consultancy, and understanding decision making that affects daily life.

sections.title: Power, authority and legitimacy
sections.html:
Concepts in political science are broad and contested, so define your terms clearly, use them consistently, and do not assume others share your meaning.

Power

Power is as central to politics as scarcity is to economics. It is the ability of A to get B to do something B would not otherwise have done, usually against opposition. It is a social relationship, not a thing you can touch. Power in use is exercised; power not in use but available is potential. Power is not necessarily negative and is not the same as physical force.

Force (the stick)Exchange (the deal)Obligation (the kiss)
Says"Do what I want or else""Do what I want and I'll do what you want""Do it because you love, respect or are committed to me"
NatureCoercive threatsProductive exchangesIntegrative relationships
Motive for obeyingFearGainCommitment
InstitutionsMilitary, policeEconomicSocial (church, family)
  • "The stick which stays in the cupboard is the biggest stick of all": an implicit threat is often the most effective.
  • Exchange: a "contract" between citizens and state. Citizens obey and pay taxes; the state provides education, health care and protection. When the state gives as well as takes, people obey more and the regime is more stable.
  • Real political power combines all three. Taxation: people pay because of coercion (fear of being caught), exchange (services) and obligation (what if everyone evaded?).

Authority

Authority is the right to rule: it exists when subordinates accept the right of superiors to give orders. Accepting authority does not mean agreeing with a decision; it means accepting the right to decide and your duty to obey (e.g. COVID-19 lockdowns). The key question is how to convert power into authority.

Max Weber's typeBasisExample
TraditionalCustom and long-established tradition; legitimate because it has 'always existed'Chiefs, kings and queens (monarchy)
CharismaticAn individual's personality: charm that inspires loyalty, devotion and emotional dependence. Short-lived unless transferred to a permanent officeHitler; many revolutionary leaders
Legal-rationalClearly defined legal rules; attached to the office, not the person; typical of modern states; limits abuse of powerThe President of Botswana; bureaucracy

Legitimacy

Legitimacy is rightful power: a widespread conviction that a government has the moral and legal right to govern. We speak of the legitimacy of a regime but the authority of an official. Legitimacy can come from elections, tradition or religion. It explains not why people should obey but why they do.

Legitimacy and performance are reciprocal. Good performance builds a reservoir of legitimacy that helps a democracy survive crises; and the more people believe in the regime's legitimacy, the better it performs.

sections.title: Political culture and socialisation
sections.html:
Political culture is the underlying set of values and beliefs about politics shared in a society: a system of meaning for interpreting politics, including attitudes, skills, norms and, in broader approaches, symbols, rituals and discourses. Almond and Verba saw it mainly as a set of psychological orientations.

Assumptions

  • Attitudes are supra-individual (shared patterns), not reducible to individuals, and can explain behaviour.
  • They come from socialisation; early learning conditions later learning ("one orients one's life by following old road maps").
  • They are shaped by history and memory and resist short-term change.
Almond's typeAwarenessParticipation
ParochialLowLittle involvement
SubjectAware of government and obligationsNo participation (rights not used)
ParticipantAwareInvolved: trust, pride in institutions, sense of competence, active in associations
CivicAware and involvedParticipation balanced by some passivity and tradition (e.g. Britain)

Components of political culture

  1. Social relations and authority: do the masses accept elite authority?
  2. Group vs individual: does the collective matter more than the individual?
  3. Liberty vs security: strong interventionist state, or freedom from the state?
  4. Political system legitimacy: is the regime accepted as having the right to rule?
  5. Political community: strong attachment to national identity?

Sources of political culture

  • Defining events: dramatic shocks that overwhelm culture's resistance to change (e.g. 9/11).
  • Repeated experiences over a long time.
  • Socialisation; globalisation may also play a part. Individual life experiences rarely change culture.

Political socialisation

The process by which individuals learn about the political system and society transmits its political culture from generation to generation. It can build loyalty or alienation. People acquire cognitive (knowledge), affective (feelings) and evaluational (judgements) orientations.

AgentRole
FamilyPrimary agent: orientations learned early are intense. Modernity weakens the family's link to politics
Peer groupsClose associates of roughly equal status; build interaction and decision-making skills; urbanised members pass on political information
ChurchInstils good conduct, respect and loyalty
SchoolSeen by some as more important than the family; the state designs the curriculum (patriotism, service)
Mass mediaNewspapers, TV, radio give information for evaluating the system; governments sometimes censor it
Political partiesSeek state power, so they shape attitudes through propaganda and debate
Adult experienceDirect experience of the political system itself

sections.title: Human rights
sections.html:
Origins

  • Ideas go back to Thomas Hobbes and John Locke. Locke's natural-law doctrine: people have a natural right to life, liberty and property.
  • 1689: the English Parliament turned these natural rights into law.
  • Locke influenced the US Constitution and the French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen ("men are born free and equal in rights").
  • 10 December 1948: the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (the UN was formed in 1945 after World War II's huge loss of life). Article 1: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights."

What human rights are

A right is a claim or justly entitled benefit. Human rights are inalienable: people are born with them; they are not given by government, president or parliament, and apply regardless of gender, colour, race, nationality or religion.

Civil and political rightsSocial, economic and cultural rights
Recognised as long as democratic society has existed; in Botswana's Bill of RightsRecognised later, once it was clear political rights mean little without them
Life and security of person; freedom from slavery; freedom from torture and cruel punishment; property; marriage and family; fair trial; privacySocial security; work and trade unions; rest and leisure; education; adequate standard of living; cultural life

UN Resolution 32/130 of 1977 (shown on the slide as 22/130): all rights are indivisible and interdependent; civil and political rights cannot be fully realised without economic, social and cultural rights.

Protecting rights

  • Botswana: Chapter 2 of the Constitution, sections 3–16, protects fundamental rights for all regardless of colour, race or sex. The constitution protects rights; it is not their source. Section 18 lets a person go to court when a right is violated.
  • Rights are not absolute: even the right to life can be lawfully taken in limited cases, and one person's rights must not infringe others' or the public interest.
  • Internationally: treaties and conventions, and humanitarian intervention by the UN when governments fail to stop gross violations.

Violations

  • Killing, torture and detention without trial (Zimbabwe, Uganda); rigged elections and intimidation of opposition (Kenya, Congo Brazzaville, Burundi); discrimination in employment by ethnicity, politics or religion.
  • Refugees: people grossly and persistently denied rights who flee to other countries. Prisoners of conscience: people jailed for their political beliefs (China, North Korea).
  • States must respect rights and create conditions for enjoying them. Rights are a pre-condition for development and the rule of law; strengthening institutions, civil society and public awareness helps.

sections.title: Political parties and party types
sections.html:
Origins

Parties are a recent invention: the earliest emerged from legislatures in the 19th century, and modern parties began in the USA. By the 1950s–60s, 80% of states were ruled by parties; in the 1960s–70s party rule declined as military rule spread, because parties were seen as divisive and as failing to solve ethnic and poverty problems.

Definitions

  • An organisation that states policy positions and runs candidates for office.
  • Downs (1957): "a coalition of men seeking to control the governing apparatus by legal means".
  • White (2006): an autonomous group of citizens that makes nominations and contests elections hoping to control government by capturing public office.

Parties seek state power alone or in coalition, nominate and present candidates, mobilise voters, stress how their programmes differ, and are the crucial link between citizens and government.

School of thoughtSees parties as…
BehaviourismDependent variables performing social functions
Rational choiceInstruments of political entrepreneurs
New institutionalismAutonomous actors interacting with a structured environment

Functions

  • Representation (the primary function): responding to and voicing the views of members and voters.
  • Interest articulation and aggregation: voicing business, labour and minority interests, and balancing competing ones.
  • Formation of government: stability, coherence, cooperation between parliament and executive.
  • Accountability: opposition criticism and debate.
  • Socialisation, mobilisation and education: parties set the agenda and shape political culture.
  • Elite recruitment: providing the state's leaders.

Why parties beat individuals for accountability: a long time horizon; they coordinate branches of government; they link candidates in different places; they cut the number of choices and so voters' decision costs.

Party government: decisions made by elected party officials; policy decided within parties; parties act cohesively; officials recruited and held accountable by parties.

TypeFeaturesExamples
Cadre partyBegan as parties of notables; now professional members, strong discipline, an elite giving ideological leadershipChinese Communist Party, Nazi Party, Fascist Party
Mass partyBroad membership and wide electoral base; recruitment-minded, less ideologicalEuropean socialist parties, BDP, ANC
Catch-all partyAppeals to the largest possible number of votersGerman Social Democrats, Labour Party
Left-wingChange through social reform or economic transformation; supported by the poor and working classSocialist, progressive, communist parties; EFF
Right-wingConservative; upholds the existing social order and continuity; supported by business and the middle classConservative parties

sections.title: Elections, voting and electoral systems
sections.html:
An election is a way of filling an office through choices made by an electorate. It is a necessary but not sufficient condition for representation. Elections differ by office, eligibility, how votes are cast and the nature of competition; how they are run is the electoral system.

Functions of elections: recruiting politicians, making governments, providing representation, influencing policy, educating voters and building legitimacy.

Voting behaviour

Why and how people vote. Short-term influences: the economy, a politician's personality, the mass media.

Theory of votingPeople vote…
Party identificationFor 'their' party, often their family's party
Rational choiceOn economic and programme assessment: which party serves my interests?
Sociological modelWith their group: peers, class

Primary elections are intra-party elections to choose candidates; general/national elections decide the next government.

Electoral systems

First past the post (FPTP)Proportional representation (PR)
How it worksVote for a candidate in a constituency; the candidate with a plurality wins; no thresholdCountry is one constituency; vote for a party; seats in proportion to votes, filled from party lists in order; threshold of at least 5%
Used inUSA, UK, India, BotswanaMany Latin American democracies (with presidentialism)
AdvantagesClear link between MP and constituents; clear choice of government; stable government; clear mandateFair to all parties; promotes national unity; includes women and minorities; many parties take part
DisadvantagesWastes votes; under-represents small parties; limited choice (two-party tendency); can undermine legitimacyWeak, unstable coalition governments; no constituency link; unpopular list candidates; centralised parties and patron–client lists

Pairings: FPTP + presidential = USA; FPTP + parliamentary = Westminster democracy; PR + presidential = Latin America.

sections.title: The military and politics
sections.html:
Military organisations developed in Europe from the Middle Ages and became professional around the 19th century. The military is a political institution of a very particular kind.

Four distinguishing features

  1. An instrument of war with a monopoly of weapons and coercive power; its loyalty is crucial to the state's survival.
  2. Tightly organised and highly disciplined: a hierarchy of ranks and a culture of strict obedience.
  3. A distinctive set of values and culture preparing soldiers to fight, kill and die.
  4. A repository of the national interest, guaranteeing the state's security and integrity.

National security (Molomo and Tsie, 1994): the maintenance, safeguarding and protection of a country's national interests (life, property and territorial integrity) from internal or external threats. Military loyalty and discipline can seem at odds with civil liberties, but its role need not clash with democracy.

Military rule in the Third World

Third-world states were prone to coups because of underdeveloped constitutions, low literacy and weak political cultures. Coups were common in Africa (especially West Africa), Latin America, the Far East and the Middle East.

RegionCoups 1960–1982
Africa25
Far East20
Latin America15
Middle East14

Coups have declined with democratisation, but the army is never fully detached from politics.

Character of military rule

  • Suspension of the constitution; dissolution of government and parliament
  • Parties banned and leaders detained
  • A military council holds authority; rule by decree, commands and directives
  • Reliance on the existing bureaucracy and an alliance with the police
  • Appeals to previously marginalised groups to gain legitimacy
  • No better than civilian rule: corruption and human rights abuses

Why the military takes over

  • The army feels the government is not serving the nation (often a cover for military interests)
  • The army is too close to the ruling party (e.g. Zimbabwe), or lacks professionalism and neutrality
  • Threats to army cohesion, e.g. dismissing officers on ethnic grounds
  • Intense social divisions; an atmosphere of illegitimacy
  • Civilian government loses legitimacy, especially by failing to deliver economic benefits

o: large-scale loss of life in World War II

qs.q: People who are grossly and persistently denied their rights and flee to other countries are
qs.x: The answer is: refugees.

qs.q: People imprisoned because of their political beliefs are called
qs.x: Examples given: China, North Korea.

qs.q: Rigged elections and intimidation of opposition supporters are given as examples of rights violations in
qs.x: The answer is: Kenya, Congo Brazzaville and Burundi.

qs.q: When governments fail to deal with gross violations of rights, the UN may
qs.x: The answer is: intervene on humanitarian grounds.

qs.q: The lecture concludes that human rights should be treated as
o: a pre-condition for development and the rule of law
qs.x: The answer is: a pre-condition for development and the rule of law.

qs.q: Which thinkers are named as early writers on human rights?
qs.x: The answer is: John Locke and Thomas Hobbes.

qs.q: The earliest political parties emerged in the 19th century from
qs.x: The answer is: legislatures.

qs.q: Modern political parties first emerged in
qs.x: The answer is: the USA.

qs.q: By the 1950s and 60s, about what share of the world's states were ruled by political parties?
qs.x: The answer is: 80%.

qs.q: Why did party rule decline in the 1960s and 1970s?
o: Military rule spread, as parties were seen as divisive and failing to solve ethnic and poverty problems
Parties were banned by the UN
qs.x: The answer is: Military rule spread, as parties were seen as divisive and failing to solve ethnic and poverty problems.

qs.q: Anthony Downs (1957) defined a party as
o: a coalition of men seeking to control the governing apparatus by legal means
an autonomous group making nominations and contesting elections
a group that seeks to influence policy without seeking office
qs.x: The second definition is White's (2006).

qs.q: What separates a party from a pressure group, according to the definitions?
o: A party seeks to win public office and control government
A party never takes part in elections
qs.x: The answer is: A party seeks to win public office and control government.

qs.q: Which school of thought sees parties as instruments of political entrepreneurs?
qs.x: The answer is: Rational choice.

qs.q: New institutionalism sees parties as
o: autonomous actors interacting with a structured environment
qs.x: The answer is: autonomous actors interacting with a structured environment.

qs.q: What is described as the primary function of political parties?
qs.x: The answer is: Representation.

qs.q: Voicing the demands of business, labour and minority groups, and balancing them, is
qs.x: The answer is: interest articulation and aggregation.

qs.q: Providing the state with its leaders is the party function of
qs.x: The answer is: elite recruitment.

qs.q: Parties hold government to account mainly through
qs.x: The answer is: opposition criticism and political debate.

qs.q: Which is a reason parties are better than individuals for accountability?
o: They reduce the number of alternatives, cutting voters' decision costs
They have a short time horizon
They work only in one locality
They avoid coordinating branches of government
qs.x: Parties also have a long time horizon and link candidates across localities.

qs.q: Under party government
o: policies are decided within parties, which act cohesively
parties have no role in policy
officials are not accountable to parties
qs.x: The answer is: policies are decided within parties, which act cohesively.

qs.q: A party dominated by an elite offering ideological leadership to the masses, with strong discipline, is a
qs.x: The answer is: cadre party.

qs.q: Which are given as examples of cadre parties?
o: The Chinese Communist Party, the Nazi Party and the Fascist Party
The German Social Democrats and Labour
qs.x: The answer is: The Chinese Communist Party, the Nazi Party and the Fascist Party.

qs.q: A party with broad-based membership and a wide electoral base, such as the BDP or ANC, is a
qs.x: The answer is: mass party.

qs.q: A party that tries to appeal to the largest possible number of voters is a
qs.x: Examples: German Social Democrats, Labour Party.

qs.q: Left-wing parties are characterised by
o: commitment to change through social reform or economic transformation
qs.x: The answer is: commitment to change through social reform or economic transformation.

qs.q: Right-wing parties typically draw support from
o: business interests and the middle class
the poor and the working class
qs.x: The answer is: business interests and the middle class.

qs.q: The EFF and MELS are given as examples of
qs.x: The answer is: left-wing parties.

qs.q: Cadre parties originally began as
o: parties of notables dominated by an informal group of leaders
qs.x: The answer is: parties of notables dominated by an informal group of leaders.

qs.q: Parties form a crucial link between
qs.x: The answer is: citizens and government.

qs.q: An election is
o: a way of filling an office through choices made by an electorate
the appointment of officials by the president
qs.x: The answer is: a way of filling an office through choices made by an electorate.

qs.q: Elections are described as which kind of condition for representation?
qs.x: The answer is: Necessary but not sufficient.

qs.q: Which is NOT one of the functions of elections listed in the lecture?
qs.x: Suspending the constitution is a feature of military rule.

qs.q: The economy, a politician's personality and the mass media are
qs.x: The answer is: short-term influences on voting.

qs.q: Voting for the party your family has always supported fits which theory?
qs.x: The answer is: Party identification.

qs.q: Voting after assessing which party's economic programme serves your interests fits which theory?
qs.x: The answer is: Rational choice.

qs.q: Voting with your class or peer group fits the
qs.x: The answer is: sociological model.

qs.q: An election held within a party to choose its candidates is a
qs.x: The answer is: primary election.

qs.q: A general (national) election determines
qs.x: The answer is: the next government.

qs.q: Under first past the post, the winner is the candidate with
o: a plurality of votes in the constituency
at least 50% of the national vote
qs.x: No threshold is needed.

qs.q: Which electoral system does Botswana use?
qs.x: Also the USA, UK and India.

qs.q: Which is an advantage of first past the post?
o: A clear link between representatives and constituents
It is fair to all parties
qs.x: The answer is: A clear link between representatives and constituents.

qs.q: Which is a disadvantage of first past the post?
o: It wastes votes and under-represents small parties
It weakens the link between MPs and constituencies
qs.x: The answer is: It wastes votes and under-represents small parties.

qs.q: First past the post tends to produce
qs.x: The answer is: two dominant parties (duopolistic tendencies).

qs.q: Under proportional representation, voters vote for
qs.x: The answer is: a party.

qs.q: Under proportional representation, the country is treated as
qs.x: The answer is: a single constituency.

qs.q: What threshold is usually imposed under proportional representation?
qs.x: The answer is: At least 5% of the vote.

qs.q: Under PR, seats are filled from party lists
qs.x: The answer is: in descending order.

qs.q: Which is an advantage of proportional representation?
o: It promotes the inclusion of women and minority candidates
It gives a strong constituency link
It wastes no time on lists
qs.x: The answer is: It promotes the inclusion of women and minority candidates.

qs.q: Which is a disadvantage of proportional representation?
o: Weak, unstable government because of many small parties
It limits voter choice to two parties
qs.x: The answer is: Weak, unstable government because of many small parties.

qs.q: Westminster democracy combines
o: first past the post with a parliamentary system
proportional representation with a presidential system
first past the post with a presidential system
qs.x: FPTP + presidential = USA; PR + presidential = Latin America.

qs.q: Latin American democracy is typically associated with
o: first past the post and parliamentarism
first past the post and presidentialism
qs.x: The answer is: proportional representation and presidentialism.

qs.q: Under PR, centralised parties can lead to
o: patron–client relationships to get on the party list
qs.x: The answer is: patron–client relationships to get on the party list.

qs.q: The military became specialised with professional leadership around the
qs.x: Military organisations date from the Middle Ages in Europe.

qs.q: Which feature distinguishes the military from other institutions?
o: A monopoly of weapons and coercive power
Freedom for members to disobey orders
qs.x: The answer is: A monopoly of weapons and coercive power.

qs.q: The military's internal structure is best described as
o: a hierarchy of ranks with a culture of strict obedience
qs.x: The answer is: a hierarchy of ranks with a culture of strict obedience.

qs.q: The military is called a repository of the national interest because it
o: guarantees the security and integrity of the state
qs.x: The answer is: guarantees the security and integrity of the state.

qs.q: Molomo and Tsie (1994) define national security as protecting national interests from
qs.x: Life, property and territorial integrity.

qs.q: Why can the military seem at odds with democracy?
o: Its unquestioning loyalty and discipline run against individual freedom and civil liberties
It refuses to protect the state
qs.x: But the lecture says its role need not clash with democratic practice.

qs.q: Third-world countries were more vulnerable to military takeovers because of
o: underdeveloped constitutions, low literacy and weak political cultures
qs.x: The answer is: underdeveloped constitutions, low literacy and weak political cultures.

qs.q: Between 1960 and 1982, how many coups were there in Africa?
qs.x: Latin America 15, Far East 20, Middle East 14.

qs.q: Which region had 15 coups between 1960 and 1982?
qs.x: The answer is: Latin America.

qs.q: Why has the number of coups declined?
qs.x: The answer is: Democratisation.

qs.q: Which part of Africa is said to still see frequent military rule?
qs.x: The answer is: West Africa.

qs.q: Which is a feature of military rule?
qs.x: The answer is: Suspension of the constitution.

qs.q: Under military rule, authority is usually vested in
qs.x: The answer is: a military council.

qs.q: Military regimes govern mainly by
qs.x: The answer is: decree, commands and directives.

qs.q: To run the state, military regimes typically rely on
o: the existing bureaucracy and an alliance with the police
qs.x: The answer is: the existing bureaucracy and an alliance with the police.

qs.q: How do military regimes try to increase their legitimacy?
o: By appealing to previously marginalised groups
qs.x: The answer is: By appealing to previously marginalised groups.

qs.q: The lecture's verdict on military regimes compared with civilian ones is that they are
o: no better: they also suffer corruption and human rights abuses
qs.x: The answer is: no better: they also suffer corruption and human rights abuses.

qs.q: An army that claims the government is 'not serving the nation well' may be using this as
o: a cover for its own military interests
qs.x: The answer is: a cover for its own military interests.

qs.q: Which country is given as an example of an army too close to the ruling party?
qs.x: The answer is: Zimbabwe.

qs.q: Dismissing army officers on tribal or ethnic grounds can trigger a coup because it
qs.x: The answer is: affects cohesion in the army.

qs.q: A civilian government is most likely to lose legitimacy, inviting a coup, when it
o: fails to deliver material economic benefits
qs.x: The answer is: fails to deliver material economic benefits.

qs.q: What makes the military less likely to intervene in politics?
o: Professionalisation and political neutrality of the army
Close ties to the ruling party
qs.x: The answer is: Professionalisation and political neutrality of the army.

qs.q: Disbanding parties and detaining party leaders is a feature of
qs.x: The answer is: military rule.
